title: Tiered Citizenship Ritual and Ceremony: The Bureaucracy of Belonging
body:
In GLMZ, citizenship is not a birthright but a administered status, renewed, upgraded, or revoked through a layered system of corporate and municipal assessments. The formal moment of tier assignment — called a Classification Review — has evolved over decades from a mundane administrative appointment into a ritualized event weighted with social meaning. Families in the Outer Ring districts treat a child's first Classification Review at age fourteen as a coming-of-age milestone, comparable to older religious confirmation rites. Parents save for months to dress children in neutral-tone business attire, a sartorial tradition rooted in the folk belief that presenting as Tier-3 Middle will bias the biometric mood assessors toward favorable scoring.

The Classification Centers themselves are architecturally designed to communicate hierarchy. The Tier-1 and Tier-2 assessment wings of the Lakefront Administrative Complex on Meridian's north shore feature climate-controlled waiting rooms with curated ambient sound and complimentary nutrient beverages. Tier-4 and Tier-5 applicants — the provisional and stateless — queue in open-air concrete antechambers called 'the apron,' exposed to weather and observable from elevated transit lines above. This spatial humiliation is not incidental; urban design historians at the Meridian Institute have documented that the apron configuration was deliberately preserved through three rounds of facility renovation. The architecture is a message.

Beyond the formal review, citizenship tier permeates daily ritual in ways that are simultaneously mundane and devastating. Tier-3 households hold 'maintenance dinners' — informal gatherings where families review each member's civic score metrics together before the quarterly update window closes. Score-adjacent behaviors — volunteer hours logged on the Municipal Contribution Ledger, transit punctuality records, purchase histories flagged as 'civically aligned' — are discussed, strategized, and sometimes gamed. Children learn to read civic score dashboards before they learn to cook. The dinner table becomes a performance review.

Counter-rituals have emerged in the lower tiers. In the Burnside Flats and the Calumet Stack districts, Tier-4 communities practice a tradition called 'the blank,' in which residents collectively disable or obscure their civic score displays on the last day of each month. It is a gesture of refusal, legally ambiguous but rarely prosecuted because enforcement resources in those districts are stretched thin. The blank has become a social occasion — music, shared food cooked on portable induction rigs, and an unspoken acknowledgment that the number on the screen is not the whole of the person.
headings: Classification Review as Rite of Passage
